entries.title: How do lungs get oxygen into your body?
entries.answer: When you breathe in, air travels down your windpipe and through branches that get smaller and smaller inside your lungs. At the ends of many branches are clusters of tiny air sacs. Oxygen from the air passes through the thin walls of those sacs and into the blood. A gas called carbon dioxide moves the other way, from blood into the sacs. When you breathe out, some of that carbon dioxide leaves your body. Your heart keeps sending blood past the sacs so it can pick up oxygen.

sections.heading: The muscle underneath
sections.text: A broad muscle called the diaphragm moves down when it tightens, making more room in your chest so air flows into the lungs.

facts: The tiny air sacs are called alveoli.
The left lung is a little smaller than the right, leaving room for the heart.

entries.title: How do muscles move your bones?
entries.answer: When you bend your elbow, muscles near your upper arm put a pull on your bones. Strong strips called tendons attach many muscles to bones. A muscle can shorten and pull, a bit like someone tugging a rope. It cannot push the bone back the other way. To straighten your elbow, a muscle toward the back of your upper arm can pull in another direction. Muscles throughout your body work together to help you stand upright, pick things up, and move without toppling over.
facts: The biceps helps bend the elbow.
The triceps helps straighten the elbow.

entries.title: How do your ears hear?
entries.answer: A sound sends vibrations through the air. When those vibrations reach your ear, they make a thin part called the eardrum move. Three tiny bones carry the movement farther into the ear. It makes waves in liquid inside the cochlea, a spiral-shaped part of the inner ear. Tiny hair cells respond to this motion and help turn it into signals. A nerve carries those signals to your brain. Your brain makes sense of them as sounds, such as a dog barking or a bell ringing.

sections.heading: Different pitches
sections.text: Different parts of the cochlea respond especially well to different pitches, from a deep drum to a high whistle.

facts: The three tiny bones are in the middle ear.
The cochlea is filled with fluid.

entries.title: How does your brain send messages?
entries.answer: Reaching for a pencil starts with messages traveling between nerve cells. A nerve cell is called a neuron. Electrical signals travel along a neuron, and chemical messengers can pass information across tiny gaps to other cells. Signals from your eyes help your brain work out where the pencil is. Signals from your brain and spinal cord help tell your arm and hand muscles how to move. Neurons also take part in things such as remembering a story or hearing a friend say your name.

sections.heading: Parts have different jobs
sections.text: Areas near the back of your brain help make sense of what you see. Other areas help plan movement, process sound, or remember what happened.

facts: The spinal cord carries many messages between the brain and body.
Your brain does jobs you do not have to think about, including helping control your breathing.

entries.title: How does your heart move blood?
entries.answer: Put a hand over your chest and you may feel your heart beating. Each beat is a squeeze from a muscle about the size of your fist. The right side sends blood to your lungs to pick up oxygen. The left side sends that blood out to the rest of your body. Each side has a room where blood arrives and another room that pushes blood out. Small flaps called valves open and close so the blood keeps moving in the right direction.

sections.heading: Two trips, one pump
sections.text: Blood returning from the body takes a short trip through the lungs, then comes back to the heart for the trip around the body.

facts: An electrical signal helps time each beat.

quiz.question: Where does the right side of your heart send blood next?
quiz.explanation: The right side sends blood to the lungs, where the blood can pick up oxygen.

entries.title: What do your kidneys do?
entries.answer: Your kidneys help keep the right mix of water, salts, and other materials in your blood. Inside each kidney, tiny filters take some water and small materials out of blood. The kidneys then send much of the water and useful materials back. Extra water and some waste leave the kidneys as urine. Thin tubes carry urine to the bladder, where it stays until you pee. These filters work all day, even when you are sleeping or thinking about something else.

sections.heading: A filter plus a return trip
sections.text: A nephron is one of the kidney’s tiny working units. It includes a filter and a tube that gives the body a chance to take back useful material.

facts: A healthy kidney has about a million nephrons.

entries.title: Where does food go after you swallow it?
entries.answer: Digestion begins before you swallow. Your teeth break up food, and saliva starts breaking down some of it. After you swallow, muscles squeeze food down a tube to your stomach. There it gets churned together with digestive juices. The mixture then moves into your small intestine. There, more juices break food into tiny pieces your body can use, and most nutrients pass out through the intestine wall. Your large intestine takes up water from what is left, and some of the leftovers eventually leave your body as poop.

sections.heading: Food moves even when you lie down
sections.text: Muscles in the wall of the food tube squeeze in waves. This helps push swallowed food along, even when gravity is not pulling it straight down.

facts: The food tube is called the esophagus.
Most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine.
